channel.title: Thirsty Planet
channel.description: Understanding water, before it's gone. The hidden water inside everyday things, the water industry in plain words, and the places already solving it.

item.title: Thirsty Places: Tokyo
item.description:
Tokyo loses about three percent of its water to leaks. London loses about a fifth, and most cities on this site lose a third or more. The difference has nothing to do with the geology or the rain. It comes from sixty years of a waterworks replacing every cast iron main under the largest city on Earth with ductile iron and steel, welding the joints, and sending crews out at night with listening rods to hear the water escaping before it reaches the surface.
The reason it started was a drought. In the summer of 1964, with the Olympic Games weeks away, the reservoirs in the hills ran dry, the city cut supply by half, and the newspapers called it the Tokyo desert. The city built the dams and canals on the Tone river that now supply four fifths of it, and then set about not wasting what they delivered.
Under the suburbs to the north is the other half of the answer: the largest storm drain in the world, five shafts seventy metres deep joined by a tunnel, that swallows a flood and pumps it into the river so the city does not have to.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Monterrey
item.description:
In the summer of 2022 the richest industrial city in Mexico turned its water on at four in the morning and off at ten. Monterrey, five million people at the foot of the Sierra Madre, brews a large share of the country's beer, rolls its steel and bottles its drinks, and it drinks from three dams in the dry hills around it. By June one of them, Cerro Prieto, was a cracked mud flat with the old road to a drowned village showing through it, and the second, La Boca, was at a tenth.
The city's answer was the rota: six hours of pressure a day, then nothing, for months, with the poor neighbourhoods on the hills getting less than six because the pressure never reached them, tankers in the streets, and protests at the gates of the bottling plants. The breweries and the soft drink plants, which hold water concessions older than the crisis, became the summer's villains, and the largest of them gave their water to the city under the cameras.
The rains of a September storm filled the dams in a week. The city is now building its fourth dam and a second aqueduct from the one reservoir that did not fail.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Delhi
item.description:
Every May in Delhi the same pictures return: a crowd around a tanker with buckets and jerrycans, a woman climbing onto its roof to get the hose first, a child under the tap of a truck that has come late. The capital of India has more than thirty million people in its region and a water board that supplies, on a good day, about three quarters of what it says the city needs. The rest comes by tanker, from private wells and from nowhere.
The sources are a river that arrives already divided, the Yamuna, which the states upstream take from before Delhi sees it; canals from the Ganga and from the Punjab that cross Haryana, with whom the city goes to court every dry year; and wells, which the south of the city has sunk to a hundred metres as the water table fell. Below the city the river is a drain: twenty two kilometres of the Yamuna, two percent of its length, carries most of its pollution, and at the barrage the foam stands a metre deep.
The city has built sewage works for forty years and connected less than half of itself to them. The river is where the rest goes.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Maize
item.description:
Maize is the most grown grain on Earth, over a billion tonnes a year, and most of it is never eaten by a person. It becomes the feed behind the chicken, the pork and the beef on this site, the ethanol in an American fuel tank, and the syrup in the drinks. A kilogram carries about 1,200 litres of water, less than rice or wheat, because the Corn Belt grows it on rain.
The small number hides two large ones. Where the rain runs out, on the High Plains of Nebraska, Kansas and Texas, the circles of sprinkler irrigated maize are drawing down the aquifer under them by a metre a year. And the nitrogen fertiliser that makes the yields possible washes off the fields into the Mississippi and, every summer, makes a dead zone the size of a small country in the Gulf of Mexico. The grey water of maize, the water needed to dilute that, is larger per kilogram than for any other grain.
A tortilla is about 40 litres. A litre of corn ethanol, counted back to the field, is about 2,000.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Golf Courses
item.description:
From the air, a golf course in the desert looks like what it is: fifty hectares of lawn in a place that has none. The Coachella Valley east of Palm Springs has more than a hundred and twenty of them, and a course there uses about a million gallons of water a day in summer, close to four thousand cubic metres, which is what a town of ten thousand people uses. The valley's courses together take a share of its water that the farms and the cities notice.
Grass does not care what it is used for. A fairway transpires like a lawn, the lawns article on this site has the numbers, and in a hot dry climate it needs one and a half to two metres of water a year. The industry has cut that by replacing turf with gravel, watering only the fairways and greens, and switching from drinking water to treated sewage and canal water, and the best desert courses now use half what they did in 1990.
On the coast of Scotland, where the game began, a links course is watered by the rain and the greens get a hose. The game is the same. The grass is not what the place can grow.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Aluminium
item.description:
Aluminium starts as red earth. Bauxite is dug in Australia, Guinea, Brazil and Jamaica, shipped to a refinery, and boiled in caustic soda until the aluminium in it dissolves and the rest, the iron that made it red, settles out as a mud. Four tonnes of bauxite make two tonnes of white alumina and one tonne of metal, and leave about one and a half tonnes of red mud, wet and caustic, stored in ponds behind dams. The world's stock of it has passed four billion tonnes.
In October 2010 the dam of one such pond at Ajka in Hungary broke and a million cubic metres of red mud ran through two villages, killed ten people, burned a hundred and fifty with its alkali, and turned the river below it dead for its whole length to the Danube.
The smelter that turns alumina into metal uses little water itself and a great deal of electricity, which is why smelters stand beside dams in Iceland, Norway and Quebec, and the reservoir behind the dam is the water in the can. A recycled can skips the mine, the mud and most of the power.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Dates
item.description:
A kilogram of dates carries about 2,300 litres of water, and more than half of it came out of the ground through a pump. Almost every other crop on this site drinks mostly rain. The date palm grows where it hardly rains at all, in the oases of Arabia, the Sahara, Iraq and Iran, and it drinks like a tree in a wet climate, a few hundred litres a day in a Gulf summer, all of it irrigation.
For three thousand years the oases managed that with springs and the underground channels that carry mountain water across the desert by gravity. The last fifty years replaced them with diesel pumps into aquifers that filled in the ice age and are not refilling, so that the palm groves of Saudi Arabia, the Emirates and Egypt stand on water that will run out before the trees do. Iraq, which had thirty million palms in the 1950s, has lost most of them to war, salt and neglect, and the groves of Basra on the Shatt al Arab are dying as the sea moves up the river.
The date is the crop that shows what a desert can afford. The answer is less than it is spending.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Mercury
item.description:
Mercury is the metal in an old thermometer, a silver liquid that rolls in beads across a table, and in that form a person can hold it in a bare hand. In water it becomes something else. Bacteria in mud and sediment attach a carbon to it and make methylmercury, which passes into plankton, then into the fish that eat the plankton, then into the fish that eat those, concentrating at every step, so that a large tuna carries about a million times the mercury of the sea around it. It is the one poison in water that is worst at the top of the food chain, which is where people eat.
Minamata, a fishing town on the coast of Kyushu, learned this first. A chemical factory discharged mercury into the bay from 1932 to 1968, the cats went mad and died, then the fishermen's children were born unable to walk or speak, and the company and the government took twelve years from the first diagnosis to stop the discharge. Thousands were certified as victims and tens of thousands were compensated.
The mercury in today's fish comes from coal stations and from the gold pans of small miners, carried through the air to every ocean. The treaty meant to end it was signed in Minamata in 2013.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: E. coli
item.description:
The germ that every water laboratory on Earth looks for first is one that does no harm to most of the people who carry it, and everyone carries it. Escherichia coli lives in the gut of every person and every warm blooded animal, in numbers of billions, and it lives almost nowhere else. That is why it is the test. If a single E. coli turns up in a hundred millilitres of tap water, something that came out of a gut has reached the water, and whatever else came out with it, the cholera, the typhoid, the viruses and the parasites, may have reached it too.
The limit is zero. The test is a day old by the time it is read, because the bacteria have to be grown to be counted, and that day is why a water works chlorinates on the assumption that the sample will fail rather than waiting to find out.
In Walkerton, Ontario, in May 2000, a strain of E. coli that does cause harm got into a well from a farm after a storm, the operators had been faking the chlorine records for years, seven people died and two thousand fell ill. The inquiry wrote the rules most of the English speaking world now uses.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Myth: You Need Eight Glasses of Water a Day
item.description:
Eight glasses of water a day is the health rule that everyone knows, and nobody can say where it came from. The nearest thing to a source is a 1945 American nutrition board that put an adult's water need at about two and a half litres a day and then wrote, in the next sentence, that most of that is already in the food. The second sentence fell off somewhere in the decades that followed, and two and a half litres of total water became eight glasses of plain water on top of everything else.
What the food agencies say now is close to the 1945 board. An adult needs about two to two and a half litres of water a day in total, and roughly a fifth of it arrives in food, with the coffee, the tea, the milk and the soup counting for the rest as much as a glass of water does. A study that measured actual water turnover in more than five thousand people found a range from one litre a day to six, depending on size, climate, activity and age, which is the reason a single number for everyone was never going to be right.
Thirst is the regulator, and it works. The people who need a rule are the old, the sick and the athlete in the heat.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Strawberries
item.description:
A punnet of strawberries carries about 140 litres of water, which is not much, and the strawberries in a northern supermarket in February carry a story that is. They were picked in Huelva, in the south west of Spain, which grows most of Spain's strawberries and sends Europe its winter berries, under thousands of hectares of plastic tunnels, on water pumped from an aquifer that also feeds Doñana, the largest wetland in western Europe.
A strawberry plant has shallow roots and a fruit that is nine tenths water, and grown out of season under plastic it is watered by drip every day from a well. The wells in Huelva have multiplied for thirty years, a share of them without a permit, and the water table under the marshes has fallen. The lagoons that the flamingos and the migrating birds depend on have dried in summer, including ones that had never dried before.
In 2021 the European court ruled that Spain had failed to protect the aquifer. In 2023 the regional government tried to legalise the irrigation anyway, and backed down. The berries are still picked in February.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Montevideo
item.description:
Uruguay has more fresh water per person than almost any country on Earth, a river the width of a sea on its doorstep, and a capital that in June 2023 had about ten days of drinking water left. The Paso Severino reservoir on the Santa Lucía river, which supplies Montevideo and most of the country's people, fell below two percent after three years of drought, and the state did the only thing it could do quickly: it mixed what was left with water from the Río de la Plata, which is brackish, and raised the legal limit on salt in the tap water so the mix would be legal.
For two months the water in nearly two million taps was salty enough to taste, with sodium at more than double the usual limit. The health ministry told pregnant women, people with kidney disease and heart patients to drink bottled water, the government took the tax off it, and the supermarkets ran out. The protests carried a slogan that translates as "it is not drought, it is plunder", aimed at the farms and the pulp mills that take the rivers upstream.
The rain came in August. The city is now building a second source on the estuary, which is the sea with a river in it.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Dubai
item.description:
Dubai has no river, a hundred millimetres of rain in a good year, an aquifer that is brackish and nearly spent, and nearly four million people who use more water per head than almost anyone on Earth. Almost every drop they drink was the Gulf a day earlier. The plants at Jebel Ali, next to the power station, turn more than two million cubic metres of seawater a day into drinking water, and the city would have a few days of supply in its tanks if they stopped.
For forty years the plants boiled the sea with the waste heat of the gas turbines that make the city's electricity, which is why Dubai's water and its power have always come from the same company and the same fuel. The new plants push the water through membranes instead, with a third of the energy, run on solar electricity from the desert, and the last boiling plant is being retired.
The sewage goes to two works in the desert and comes back as the water on every verge, park and golf course in the city, and as the lagoon at the end of the creek where the flamingos stand. The storm of April 2024 showed what the city had never built: drains.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Bogotá
item.description:
Bogotá drinks from a moorland. Above the city, at three and four thousand metres, lies the páramo of Chingaza, a cold wet plateau of fog, moss and a plant called the frailejón that looks like a palm crossed with a cabbage, and whose soils hold water like a sponge and let it go slowly into the rivers. Seven tenths of the capital's water is collected there, in two reservoirs, and carried down through a tunnel in the mountain.
In early 2024 El Niño dried the páramo. The Chuza reservoir fell to about 16 percent, lower than it had ever been, and on 11 April the city began rationing: eight million people divided into nine zones, each cut off for 24 hours in turn. The rota ran, with changes, for a year. People filled bathtubs and buckets on the night before their day, the car washes closed, and the city's use fell by about a tenth and stayed down.
The rains returned, the reservoirs filled, and the rationing ended in April 2025. What it taught was that a city of eight million was one dry year from the tanks on the roofs of Amman.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Irrigation
item.description:
Of all the fresh water people take out of rivers, lakes and the ground, about seven tenths goes to one thing: watering crops. Industry takes about a fifth and every city, town and household on Earth takes the rest. Irrigation is the thirsty industry that the others on this site are footnotes to.
It covers about a fifth of the world's cropland and grows about two fifths of its food, and most of it is done the way it was done in Mesopotamia: water let onto a field through a gate and left to soak in. Half of that water never reaches a plant. Sprinklers and drip lines do better, and the countries that have switched to them have mostly grown more crops on the same water rather than giving any back, which is the paradox the engineers and the economists have argued over for twenty years.
A fifth of the world's irrigated land is damaged by the salt the water leaves behind. The aquifer under the American plains, which feeds the circles seen from every flight across the country, is going down by a metre a year in Kansas and Texas. The food on the table came from one of these fields.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Hospitals
item.description:
A hospital bed uses several hundred litres of water a day in a rich country, up to a thousand in the busiest sites, which is a small household's week. Hardly any of it is drunk. It goes into the steam sterilisers, the laundry, the cooling towers, the kitchens, the hundreds of basins at which hands are washed, and the one machine that is more particular about water than any other in the building.
A dialysis machine passes about 120 litres of water across a patient's blood in a session, three times a week, and that water has to be cleaner than drinking water by a wide margin. The chlorine and chloramine that keep city water safe to drink will destroy red blood cells if they reach the dialyser, so every dialysis unit runs its own small treatment plant: carbon to strip the chlorine, reverse osmosis to strip the rest, and a loop that is tested for bacteria and endotoxin because a fever in a dialysis ward is a water fault until proved otherwise.
What goes out carries antibiotics, contrast agents and the drugs of the oncology ward, and the plant that cleans the city's sewage was not designed for them.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Banana
item.description:
A banana carries about a hundred litres of water. Most of it fell as rain on a plantation on the coast of Ecuador, which sends the world a third of the bananas it trades, or in the Philippines, Costa Rica, Colombia or Guatemala, and almost all of it went through the plant: a banana plant is a giant herb with no woody stem, and it moves water from the soil to the air faster than most trees.
Per kilogram the banana is one of the lighter footprints on this site, about 790 litres against 1,800 for a mango and 2,500 for rice, because the fruit is heavy and the plant grows fast where the rain is two metres a year. The water that matters is the smaller part: the irrigation on the dry coasts, the wash tanks of the packing station, and the forty flights a year of fungicide over the plantations of the wet countries.
Every export banana is the same plant, a clone called Cavendish, and a soil fungus that kills it has crossed from Asia to Latin America. The water will be the same for whatever replaces it.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Turbidity
item.description:
Hold a glass of water up to the light and the first thing you judge is whether you can see through it. The water industry turned that glance into a number: turbidity, measured by shining a light into the water and counting how much of it is scattered sideways by the particles it cannot pass through. The unit is the NTU, and a river in flood runs at hundreds; the water leaving a modern filter runs at a tenth.
The particles themselves, clay, silt, algae, are mostly harmless. The reason the number matters is what hides in them. A parasite like Cryptosporidium, which chlorine cannot kill, travels on and inside the particles, and a filter that lets the particles through lets the parasite through. In Milwaukee in 1993 the turbidity of the finished water rose for days, within the rules of the time, and 400,000 people fell ill. The rule in the United States is now 0.3 NTU, in 95 percent of samples, which is a cloudiness no eye can see.
The number on the plant's screen is the one the operator watches most. A rise of a few tenths is the first sign that a filter has broken through.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Septic Tanks
item.description:
About one American household in five is not on a sewer, and neither are a third of the people on Earth. The water that leaves the house goes into a buried tank in the garden, sits there for a day or two, and seeps out into the ground. Nothing on this site is older, cheaper, or more often ignored until it fails.
The tank does less than people think. The solids settle to the bottom and the grease floats, and the water in between leaves about as dirty as it came, a third cleaner at best. The real treatment is the soil under the drain field: a metre of unsaturated earth, alive with bacteria, that finishes the job the tank started before the water reaches the groundwater. A tank on clay, or on sand with the water table a few feet down, or next to the well that supplies the house, is a different story, and it is the story of the nitrate in a lot of private wells.
Multiply it by a suburb and the nitrogen reaches the bay. Cape Cod, Long Island and the Florida lagoons are learning what a hundred thousand tanks do to an estuary. The tank in the garden is a treatment plant, and almost nobody treats it as one.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Myth: Chlorine in Tap Water Is Dangerous
item.description:
Chlorine is a poison. It was used as a gas on the Western Front, a leak from a railway tanker empties a town, and a cylinder of it stands in a locked room at most of the water works in the world, from which a little is dosed into the water that comes out of your tap. The myth says that a chemical that dangerous cannot be safe to drink. The verdict is that at the dose in a glass of water it is among the safest things in the glass.
A tap carries a few tenths of a milligram of chlorine a litre. The World Health Organization's limit for a lifetime of drinking is five, and a swimming pool runs at one to three. At those doses chlorine has been studied for a century in more people than any other substance in water, and what the studies found is the opposite of the myth: when the cities of Europe and America began adding chlorine, from 1908 onward, typhoid and cholera went from the leading killers of children to diseases a doctor might never see.
The real argument is about the byproducts chlorine makes with the organic traces in water, which are regulated and which this site has covered. The chlorine itself is in the glass so that nothing else is.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Microplastics
item.description:
A study in 2024 counted the plastic in a litre of bottled water with a new laser technique and found about 240,000 pieces, ninety percent of them smaller than a micron. Earlier counts, which could only see the larger particles, had found a few hundred. The plastic was there all along. The instruments caught up.
Microplastics are in rivers, rain, the sea, the deep ocean, the air of a living room, and the blood and placentas of people who have been tested. They come from tyres wearing on roads, synthetic clothes shedding in the wash, paint, packaging, and the breakdown of everything plastic that was ever thrown away. They reach water through the sewage works, which removes most of them and sends them to the sludge, and from there to the fields.
What is known: they are everywhere and the counts rise with every better instrument. What is unknown: what they do to a body at the doses found. What is certain: a conventional treatment plant takes out most of them, and bottled water carries more than a tap. The one place where the answer is easy is the one most people get wrong.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Roses
item.description:
A rose stem from a Kenyan farm carries about ten litres of water, and there are twenty in a bunch. The flower is grown under plastic on the shore of Lake Naivasha, a freshwater lake in the Rift Valley a hundred kilometres from Nairobi, cut in the morning, chilled, packed, trucked to the airport that evening, flown to Amsterdam overnight, auctioned by lunchtime and on a shelf in London or Berlin the next day. Kenya sends Europe about a third of its roses, and most of them come from one lake.
The industry moved to the equator because the light is constant, the labour is cheap, and a greenhouse at 1,900 metres needs no heating, so that a Kenyan rose, flown, carries less carbon than a Dutch one grown under lamps in February. The water is the lake's. Naivasha fell by several metres in the 2000s as the farms drew on it and the rains failed, and the fish, the hippos and the town that drew on it too found the shore a kilometre away. It has since risen with the rains, and the farms have moved to drip and to recycling because the buyers asked.
A rose is water, air freight and a week in a vase. The water is the part that stays in Kenya.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Los Angeles
item.description:
Los Angeles gets about 380 millimetres of rain a year and has a river that runs in a concrete channel and is dry for most of it. The city exists because in 1913 it opened an aqueduct three hundred and seventy five kilometres long from the Owens valley on the far side of the Sierra Nevada, having bought the valley's water rights through agents who did not say who they worked for, and because it then reached for the Colorado in 1941 and the rivers of northern California in 1972. Every drop it drinks is imported, and every source it imports from is shrinking.
The Owens valley became a dust bowl; the lake the aqueduct drained was, for decades, the largest source of dust pollution in the United States, and the city now spends more water keeping the dust down than it takes. The Colorado, which supplies a quarter of southern California, is in its longest drought in a thousand years, and the states that share it are negotiating who loses.
The city's answer is the one Orange County and Singapore gave: recycle. The largest sewage works on the coast is being rebuilt to turn all of its outflow into drinking water by 2035, which would give the city a third of its supply from inside its own borders for the first time in a century.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Kathmandu
item.description:
Nepal has the Himalaya, eight of the world's ten highest mountains, and more fresh water per person than almost any country. Its capital gets water a few hours a week. The Kathmandu valley holds four million people in a bowl of hills, the rivers that drain it are small and, below the city, sewers, and the utility's supply in the dry season is about a third of what the valley uses. The rest comes from wells, most of them illegal, and from tankers that queue at the wells at dawn.
The answer was Melamchi: a river in the next valley, a tunnel twenty six kilometres through the hills, and a treatment works on the city's edge. It was designed in the 1980s, financed in 1998, and finished in 2021, after two decades of contractors leaving, a civil war, an earthquake and a political fight over every kilometre. Water flowed in March 2021. In June a flood on the Melamchi buried the intake under metres of debris, and the tunnel has run only in the dry months since.
The valley's wells, meanwhile, have fallen by tens of metres, the stone spouts that watered the old city for a thousand years have dried, and the tankers charge by the litre.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Amman
item.description:
In Amman the water comes one day a week. Every district has a delivery day, the pipes are pressurised for it, the tanks on every roof fill, and the household lives from the tank until the next delivery. It has been the system since the 1980s, it is how a city of four million lives in a country with about a hundred cubic metres of water a person a year, a tenth of the level the United Nations calls scarcity, and it is why every building in the city has a row of black tanks on its roof.
The water comes from wells around the city that are falling, from the King Abdullah canal that carries the Yarmouk and the Jordan's tributaries down the valley and pumps them a thousand metres up to the plateau, and, since 2013, from Disi: a fossil aquifer under the southern desert, three hundred kilometres away, tapped by fifty five wells and piped north at a hundred million cubic metres a year. The water fell as rain thirty thousand years ago. When it is used it will not come back.
About half of what enters the pipes is lost or taken without payment. A million Syrian refugees since 2011 added a fifth to the demand. The next source is the sea, at Aqaba, pumped up the length of the country.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Pasta
item.description:
A kilogram of dry pasta carries about 1,850 litres of water, and about 1,800 of them fell as rain on a field of durum wheat, in southern Italy, in Canada, in the American plains or in Kazakhstan. Durum is the hard wheat of dry country, sown where the summers are hot and the rain is scarce, and it is grown almost entirely without irrigation. The bread article on this site does the arithmetic for soft wheat; pasta's is the same, on a harder grain, with less of it eaten per meal.
Italy makes a third of the world's pasta and grows about half the durum it needs; the rest comes from Canada, whose prairies grow more of it than any country, and the water in a bowl of spaghetti in Rome is, for that share, rain on Saskatchewan. The factory adds almost nothing: a few litres a kilogram to mix and dry.
The pot adds the most that a cook ever adds to any food's footprint. The instruction on the packet, a litre of water for every hundred grams, is ten litres a kilogram, heated to the boil and poured down the sink, and the argument in Italy in 2022 about whether a Nobel laureate was right to say the pasta should be cooked with the lid on and the heat off was, at bottom, about that pot.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Ski Resorts
item.description:
The snow on most pistes in the Alps was made. Ninety percent of Italy's ski slopes and about seventy percent of Austria's are covered by artificial snow for at least part of the season, blown from cannons and lances on cold nights from water pumped out of reservoirs dug into the high pasture for the purpose. A cubic metre of water makes about two cubic metres of snow, a kilometre of piste takes several thousand cubic metres a season, and a large resort uses the water of a town of ten thousand people between November and March.
The water is not lost, mostly. It melts in spring and runs down the same streams it was pumped from, minus the share that evaporated in the making, which is a fifth to a third. What it is, is moved: taken from the streams in autumn when they are lowest, stored above the treeline in reservoirs that did not exist thirty years ago, and put back in April. The trout in the stream notice. So does the village below the reservoir if the dam fails.
The industry makes snow because the natural kind is failing at the altitudes where the resorts were built, and the snowmaking that keeps a resort open at 1,500 metres in a warm winter is also the reason it is still there to argue about.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Car Washes
item.description:
A car washed with a hose on the drive uses three to five hundred litres of water, and every litre of it, with the soap, the road grime, the brake dust and the oil, runs into the gutter and down a storm drain that leads, in most cities, straight to the river. A car washed in a modern commercial tunnel uses about a hundred and fifty litres of fresh water, because most of what touches the car has been used before, and the water that leaves goes to the sewer and the treatment works.
The industry likes to say this, and it is true. It is also the reason the car wash is the first business to be closed in a drought, because it is visible, it uses water for something nobody needs, and a city that has told its residents to stop watering the lawn cannot leave a tunnel wash running on the main road. The bans that followed the droughts in California, Cape Town and Sydney closed the washes that had spent most on reclaim and left the drive and the bucket, which use more.
The water in the car wash is small. The argument about it is the argument every dry city has in August about what water is for.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Rainwater Harvesting
item.description:
A roof of a hundred square metres in a place with six hundred millimetres of rain a year catches about sixty thousand litres, and after the first flush, the overflow and the evaporation it delivers about forty eight thousand to a tank. That is close to what a careful household of two or three uses indoors in a year, and in most of the world it runs off the roof into a downpipe and a drain and is gone.
Harvesting it is the oldest water technology there is and the least used in cities. Bermuda, which has no rivers, has required every house to catch its roof water since the seventeenth century, and the island's stepped white roofs are the catchment. Chennai made tanks compulsory on every building in 2003 after a drought, and its aquifer rose. About a quarter of Australian households have a tank, most fitted since the Millennium Drought, and in Adelaide it is half.
The water is clean enough for the garden, the toilet and the washing machine without treatment, and for drinking with a filter and a lamp. The tank is the cost. The roof is already there.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Ballast Water
item.description:
A ship that has unloaded its cargo is too light to sail safely, so it fills tanks in its hull with seawater, tens of thousands of tonnes of it, and carries the water to the port where it loads, where it pumps the water out to make room for the cargo. The world's fleet moves about five billion tonnes of water this way every year, from one sea to another, and every tonne carries whatever was in the water where it was taken on: larvae, algae, bacteria, the eggs of fish, the spores of things that had never been on the other side of an ocean.
The zebra mussel reached the Great Lakes from the Caspian in a ship's tanks in the 1980s and now coats every intake pipe and every boat hull in the basin at a cost of hundreds of millions a year. A comb jelly from the American coast reached the Black Sea the same way and ate the plankton and the fish eggs until the anchovy fishery collapsed. The list runs to hundreds of species and every ocean.
The convention that requires ships to treat their ballast before discharge was agreed in 2004 and came into force in 2017, and a ship now carries, below its waterline, a small water treatment works.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Myth: A Swimming Pool Wastes More Water Than a Lawn
item.description:
In a drought, the pool is the thing the neighbours point at. It is a tank of drinking water in the garden, it evaporates all summer, and it looks like waste. The lawn next to it, which is what the pool usually replaced, does not look like anything, and in the dry cities where both are common it uses more.
An uncovered pool in Phoenix, Perth or Los Angeles loses about a metre and a half of water a year to evaporation, plus what splashes out and what is drained for cleaning. A lawn of the same area in the same climate needs about a metre and a half to two metres of sprinkler water a year to stay green, every year, and it does not come back when the season ends. The pool is filled once, and topped up. The studies that have metered both, in Phoenix and in Perth, found the pool using the same or less than the grass it sits where.
A cover cuts the pool's evaporation by more than half. Gravel and native planting cut the lawn's water to nothing. The myth is that the pool is the waste; the honest comparison is either of them against a garden that needs no hose.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Soy
item.description:
A kilogram of soybeans carries about 2,100 litres of water, and about 95 percent of it is rain. Soy is the least irrigated of the world's great crops, grown on the summer rain of the American midwest, the Brazilian plateau and the Argentine pampas, and its footprint is green in the sense the wool and sunflower articles on this site use: water that fell on farmland and would have grown something else.
Very little of it is eaten as soy. About three quarters of the world's crop is crushed for oil and the protein meal that is left goes into the feed of pigs, chickens and farmed fish, so that most of the soy on Earth is eaten as a chicken breast or a pork chop. Tofu, soy milk, tempeh and sauce take about seven percent. A kilogram of tofu carries about 2,500 litres and replaces a kilogram of chicken at 4,300 or beef at 15,000, and a litre of soy milk carries about 300 against a cow's 1,000.
The argument about soy is about land. The crop has spread across the Cerrado, the savanna of central Brazil, faster than any crop in history, and the water it carries is the rain that fell on what was there before.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Santiago
item.description:
Santiago has been in drought since 2010. Central Chile has had a run of dry years longer than anything in its record, with rainfall a third below normal and, more important, a snowpack in the Andes that has shrunk to a fraction, because the snow is what feeds the Maipo river through the dry summer, and the Maipo is where seven million people's water comes from.
Chile is also the country where water is most completely private. The water code of 1981 made rights to water a property separate from the land, granted in perpetuity and freely traded, and the rights to most of the country's rivers were allocated in the 1980s and 1990s to farms, mines and utilities, on the assumption that the rivers would carry what they had. They do not, and the rights add up to more water than exists. A lake south of the city, Aculeo, twelve square kilometres of water with houses and boats on it, dried completely in 2018 while the rights to the streams that fed it were still being exercised upstream.
In 2022 the city's governor announced a rationing plan, the first in its history. The rain that winter was better. The drought has not ended.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Manila
item.description:
Manila drinks from one dam. The Angat reservoir, in the mountains sixty kilometres north east, supplies about ninety seven percent of the water for fourteen million people, and in a year when the rains fail it falls to the level at which the city's two water companies start turning off districts by rota. In March 2019 that happened to the eastern half of the city for weeks, with queues at fire hydrants and hospitals on tankers, while the reservoir that was supposed to take the strain, a second source planned since the 2000s, was still unbuilt.
The city is also the world's largest experiment in private water. In 1997 the state utility, which had lost two thirds of its water to leaks and theft and reached about two thirds of the city, was split into two concessions and sold. One of them cut its losses from sixty three percent to under ten, connected the slums it had been told could not be connected, and became the industry's model. The other took longer. Neither could build a dam.
The dam is now being built, in the Sierra Madre, over the objections of the people whose land it floods, and it will give the city one more source in a country of typhoons and a dry season that is getting longer.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Lahore
item.description:
Lahore is the second city of Pakistan and it drinks entirely from the ground. Every litre its utility supplies comes from more than five hundred deep wells sunk into the sand of the Punjab plain, and the water table under the city has been falling by close to a metre a year for thirty years. It was a few metres down in the 1960s. It is forty to fifty in the centre now.
The reason is the Ravi. The river that the city was built beside was allocated to India by the Indus Waters Treaty of 1960, which divided the rivers of the Punjab between the two countries, and India uses it upstream. What reaches Lahore for most of the year is the city's own sewage and the effluent of its factories, in a channel that was a river, and the city has never built a plant to treat it, because there is nothing in it to treat.
The wells are running into arsenic, as the delta's wells did in Bangladesh, and into the salt that the plain's irrigation left in the ground. The plan to replace them is a canal from the Indus system and a treatment plant, and a new city, built on the dry riverbed, that would need more water than the old one.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Olive Oil
item.description:
A litre of olive oil carries about fourteen thousand litres of water, twice sunflower oil and three times rapeseed, and for most of the tree's history nearly all of it was rain. The olive is the tree of dry country: it grows on stony hillsides with four hundred millimetres of rain a year, sends its roots deep, and gives a small crop of fruit every year and a larger one every other. The number is high because the yield is low, and the rain was falling on the hillside anyway.
That is changing. Half the world's olive oil is Spanish, most of it from Andalusia, and the groves planted since the 1990s are irrigated: hedgerows of small trees at two thousand to the hectare, watered by drip from the Guadalquivir and from wells, giving several times the yield of the old groves at a cost of a few thousand cubic metres of water per hectare in the driest region of Europe. The old groves carry rain. The new ones carry a river.
In 2022 and 2023 the rain failed in Andalusia and the harvest halved, twice. The world price of olive oil tripled, supermarkets in Spain locked the bottles, and the argument about who the Guadalquivir is for had olive oil in it for the first time.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Breweries
item.description:
A brewery uses about three litres of water for every litre of beer, and the best plants in the world are under two and a half. A generation ago it was six or seven. The beer article on this site counts the whole footprint of a glass, and the barley is nearly all of it; this one is about the plant, where the water is the process, the cleaning and the cooling, and where the effluent is a sweet, warm, oxygen hungry stream that a sewage works charges extra to take.
The industry counts its water more carefully than most, because a brewery is a large, visible user in a town, and because the largest brewers have learned what a shortage does to a licence. In 2020 the city of Mexicali, in the desert of Baja California, voted by three to one against a nearly finished brewery that would have used twenty million litres a day of the city's groundwater to make beer for export to the United States, and the plant was abandoned with the tanks in place.
The lesson the brewers drew was that the three litres in the plant are the ones that decide whether the plant exists.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Bottled Water Plants
item.description:
A bottled water plant is a well with a filling line on top. It pumps a spring or an aquifer, filters the water, treats it lightly or not at all, fills it into bottles it usually makes on site from pellets of plastic, and ships it away by truck, which is the one thing that makes it different from every other water user in the town: the water does not come back. A brewery's water returns as effluent, a farm's as drainage and rain. A bottling plant's leaves the watershed in a lorry.
The volumes are small by the standards of this site. The plant at the centre of the long fight in Michigan was permitted for about two million litres a day, the water of a town of ten thousand people, and paid the state two hundred dollars a year for the paperwork. The fight was about the price, the principle and the spring, in that order, and it ran for twenty years through the courts and the state legislature, in a state that sits on a fifth of the world's fresh surface water.
The water is not the point. The bottled water article on this site makes that case. The plant is the point, because it is where a public thing becomes a private one, a few hundred million litres at a time.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Water Meters
item.description:
When a water meter is fitted to a house that has never had one, the household's use falls by about fifteen percent, and stays down. Nobody in the house was asked to do anything. The bill that used to be a fixed charge, based on the value of the house, became a number that moved with the tap, and the tap moved.
About half the households in England still have no meter, and pay a flat charge whatever they use, which is the arrangement most of the world's cities began with and many of the poorest still have. The utility that cannot see how much each customer uses cannot find the leaks on their side of the pipe, cannot price the pool differently from the kettle, and cannot tell a household that its use has doubled since Tuesday, which is what a burst pipe under the floor looks like.
A smart meter does all three. The catch is the bill, which rises for the large household in the small house, and the politics, which in Ireland in 2016 ended the charges altogether after two years of protests.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Private Wells
item.description:
Every article in the plain water pillar of this site describes something a utility does to water before it reaches a tap: coagulation, filtration, disinfection, the tests. About forty three million Americans, one in eight, drink from a well in the garden to which none of that applies. The drinking water law stops at the public supply, and the well is the owner's, to test or not, and most do not.
When the national geological survey sampled two thousand of them, it found about one in five above a health limit for something: nitrate under farmland, arsenic and uranium where the rock carries them, radon in the granite country, bacteria where a septic tank was too close. The owners, in most cases, had never tested. The water tasted fine, and had for years, which is what arsenic and nitrate taste like.
The same is true of the private supplies of rural Britain, the wells of rural India and Bangladesh, where the arsenic article on this site began, and the boreholes of every farm on Earth. The water people trust most is the water nobody checks.
The long version is on the site.
